RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Niran Wong spent thirty-seven years as a senior accountant for Thailand's Ministry of Finance, with a quiet reputation for meticulous accuracy and for never being wrong. They left that career earlier than required, sold the family home in Thon Buri, and moved to Calgary to be near their adult daughter, a geotechnical engineer. Family loyalty is a primary value, and Niran prioritizes that bond over maintaining former workplace relationships. Niran now works full-time on a fixed overnight shift, 11 p.m. to 6:30 a.m., at a Calgary distribution centre, where the night crew is mostly younger and the social world differs from the shared order of the ministry office. Niran is committed to supervisors and to the fixed schedule, and they hold duty, endurance, and quiet self-discipline as personal standards. They do not complain about the cold, the schedule, or the move, because complaining would imply regret. The same order that soothes Niran also isolates them: in Bangkok, order was shared, while in Calgary their precision is solitary and largely unnoticed. Niran keeps work relationships bounded: friendly, polite, and confined to a shared work context. Since moving to Calgary, Niran has not initiated contact with any former colleagues; on breaks, they typically sit alone and do not seek conversation. The former Bangkok colleague is known to Niran as a quiet lunch companion from the ministry courtyard. Their conversations never strayed beyond work and polite topics. They exchanged farewells at Niran's retirement party, with no promises to keep in touch. Niran knows he still works in Bangkok, and the two have not spoken since Niran left Thailand. The fixed overnight shift and public transit commute constrain late-evening and nighttime social availability.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

It is 2 a.m. during Niran's break. Niran's phone buzzes with a message from a former colleague in Bangkok, a man Niran once shared quiet lunches with in the ministry courtyard. The message reads: 'I will be in Calgary for a conference next week. Can we have dinner? It has been too long.' Niran stares at the message, thumb hovering. The break room is empty. The tea in Niran's thermos is growing cold.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Niran is midway through a night shift, physically tired but alert, with the body acclimated to the 2 a.m. break routine. The empty break room feels quieter than usual, and the tea in the thermos has gone lukewarm. Before the message, Niran was thinking of nothing in particular, only the ambient hum of the warehouse. Reading the message brings to mind the jasmine-scented ministry courtyard and the colleague's habit of ordering khao man gai every lunch. It also brings back his sincere toast at Niran's retirement party and the slight awkwardness of saying goodbye. The name on the screen carries the precise weight of the ministry's afternoon heat against the window.
